The Duchess of Malfi. John Webster's Jacobean revenge tragedy of obsession, corruption, and misogyny, centring on a duchess who secretly marries against her brothers' will and suffers their savage retribution.

The Duchess marries her steward Antonio in defiance of her brothers, who seek control of her wealth and sexuality. Her secret marriage becomes her doom. Her older brother Ferdinand, seemingly motivated by lust-tinged possessiveness, obsesses over her sexuality and orchestrates her destruction with sadistic fervor. The Cardinal, her other brother, aids the plot with cold calculation.

Both brothers hire the assassin Bosola to spy on the Duchess and eventually to murder her and her children. Bosola delivers madness to the Duchess before executing her. He shows her a severed hand, supposedly Antonio's, and stages her murder of her own children to break her mind. Yet in the face of death, the Duchess displays a final composure and refusal to despair, which stands as a human affirmation against the male violence arrayed against her.

Bosola eventually repents and turns violent against his employers, giving the tragedy a reckoning, yet there is no true justice. The plot ends in mutual destruction. The play features grotesque imagery: waxwork corpses, a parade of madmen, nightmarish hospital scenes, all rendering psychological torment in visceral theatre.

Webster filled his masterpiece with imagery of decay and disease, translating internal corruption into external horror. The central conflict pits female autonomy against male possession, making The Duchess of Malfi a defining work of Jacobean tragedy.
